implementation_notes: Boost.Icl ships the interval vocabulary directly: dynamically bounded intervals via discrete_interval<int>::closed(a, b) / ::right_open(a, b) or the interval_bounds argument to construct(), statically bounded types (right_open_interval, left_open_interval, closed_interval, open_interval) when the convention is fixed at compile time, and interval_set / interval_map that merge, separate or split on insertion according to the combining style. Use the plain interval type when the decision is local; adopt an interval container when many intervals must be held in minimal representation and queried by overlap, because then the container - not a loop - owns the merging policy.
pitfalls: The library default changes meaning when BOOST_ICL_USE_STATIC_BOUNDED_INTERVALS is defined before the includes: the default interval type becomes right_open_interval and interval<int>::closed(a, b) then shifts the border (for discrete types) instead of storing a closed interval.
closed_interval and open_interval only work with discrete domain types; for continuous types such as double only continuous_interval can express a singleton.
interval_set and interval_map coalesce intervals that overlap or touch when their values are equal, so the input boundaries disappear: use split_interval_map when the borders carry meaning.
Concepts and diagnostics are thin - most misuse (wrong interval type for the domain type) surfaces as a template error inside the library, not at the call site.

variants.name: Hand-rolled interval struct with std::optional endpoints
variants.idiom_name: struct Interval { std::optional<T> lo, hi; bool loClosed, hiClosed; }
variants.implementation_notes: Without Boost in the stack, std::optional (C++17) is the null-endpoint way of expressing open ends that the pattern describes: std::nullopt means 'no bound on this side', and std::optional's ordering places an empty optional before any value, which keeps the comparison helpers short. Pair it with constexpr factories (closed, closedOpen, atLeast, atMost) and validate the endpoints once in the constructor, so the two flags and the two optionals are never interpreted by a caller.
pitfalls: std::optional<T> is not a bounded endpoint: default-constructed optionals silently mean 'unbounded', so an Interval built from a partially filled struct widens instead of failing.
T must have a total order; with float or pointer endpoints the NaN/unrelated-pointer comparison rules quietly break the invariant check and containment tests.

The struct grows to two optionals plus two flags, so equality and hashing must be written explicitly - and two intervals that denote the same set with different flags will compare unequal unless you canonicalise in the factory.
